title: stress-ng loaded: 0% launch success under full CPU saturation
description:
## Symptom
Under stress-ng-induced full CPU saturation on the host, all m80 launches fail. Idle launches succeed at 100 % at N=20; under stress-ng saturation the success rate drops to 0 %.

## Suspected location
Failure is downstream of phase_3 (storage prep) and is likely vsock/ready_probe contention. The warm-pool P95 also spikes to 623 ms under CPU saturation (vs 21 ms idle) due to restored-vsock retry delays — same family of contention but a less severe expression.

## Why this matters
Hermes notes flag this as "fix before GA". It is a release-gating reliability defect for any deployment that could see noisy-neighbor or burst CPU pressure. The multi-tenant pool architecture (m80-iswt) cannot be claimed reliable until this is closed.

## Investigation directions
- Add diagnostic timing to ready_probe / vsock connect path so saturation behavior is visible.
- Compare saturation behavior of cold-boot vs snapshot-restore vs warm-pool allocation (snapshot/warm may bypass the contended path).
- Check whether ready_accept timeout budgets shrink effectively under saturation (proportional vs fixed).
- Check whether host-side vsock muxer accept loop loses to higher-priority threads under saturation.

## Acceptance
- A repro script that reliably triggers the failure under stress-ng -c \$(nproc).
- A diagnosis identifying the contended resource (vsock muxer? ready_probe budget? cgroup CPU shares? scheduler class?).
- A fix bringing success rate to ≥80 % under CPU saturation, with documented residual failure modes.

## Out of scope
- Memory-pressure or disk-saturation reliability (separate investigations if needed).

Source: /tmp/m80-hermes-notes.md "Known Issues".

title: Stripped guest kernel: minimal config + cmdline trim + init-baked
description:
The firecracker-ci stock kernel takes ~890ms to reach userspace on minimal/idle (P50, m80-f2zc.7 baseline). A purpose-built kernel with the smallest config set m80 needs (vsock, virtio-blk, virtio-net, ext4, overlayfs, devtmpfs; everything else off) plus a trimmed cmdline reaches userspace in ~150-300ms typically — saving 500-700ms per cold launch.

Independent of and complementary to: storage pivot (m80-f2zc) which removes ~700ms of rootfs clone, and snapshot/restore (m80-rrp.3) which skips kernel boot entirely for warm-pool launches but still needs a fast cold boot to fill the pool.

PLAN: docs/planning/agent-roadmap.md (full sequencing).

Sub-leaves:
- DESIGN: lock the kernel config delta (CONFIGs to keep, drop, modify), build environment (Docker? chroot? upstream kernel-build container?), kernel version
- IMPL m80-image-build: kernel build pipeline producing kernels/vmlinux-m80-<sha>.bin; manifest gains a kernel.kind discriminator parallel to image_kind
- IMPL m80-firecracker: cmdline trim — quiet loglevel=0 8250.nr_uarts=0, dropped pci=off duplicate, kept reboot=k panic=-1
- BENCH: measure boot-to-guestd-bind delta on minimal/idle and minimal/loaded; target <300ms
- DOCS: manifest schema bump if needed; README delta in m80-image-build

NON-GOALS: kernel security hardening beyond what minimal CONFIG provides; multi-arch (x86_64 only in v0.2); kernel-source vendoring (use upstream linux.tar.xz).

title: DESIGN: kernel config delta + build environment + version
description:
Pin the contract:

1. Kernel version: latest LTS (5.15.x or 6.1.x) or align with firecracker-ci's track. Decide.
2. CONFIG keep list: CONFIG_VSOCKETS, CONFIG_VIRTIO_VSOCKETS, CONFIG_VIRTIO_BLK, CONFIG_VIRTIO_NET, CONFIG_VIRTIO_MMIO, CONFIG_EXT4_FS, CONFIG_OVERLAY_FS (per m80-f2zc.5), CONFIG_DEVTMPFS, CONFIG_DEVTMPFS_MOUNT, CONFIG_SERIAL_8250, CONFIG_SERIAL_8250_CONSOLE.
3. CONFIG drop list: PCI (CONFIG_PCI=n — we use virtio-mmio), most filesystems (CONFIG_BTRFS, XFS, F2FS, etc.), most network protocols (keep IPv4 only), USB, sound, drm, framebuffer, input, security modules beyond minimum, debugfs, tracing, ftrace, perf, kdb, kgdb, crash kernel.
4. Build environment: a Docker container based on Ubuntu 22.04 with kernel-build tooling (build-essential, bc, flex, bison, libelf-dev, libssl-dev). Reproducible Dockerfile committed to crates/m80-image-build/kernel-builder/.
5. Output convention: crates/m80-image-build/kernels/vmlinux-m80-<config-sha>.bin; manifest schema gains kernel.kind variant.

title: streaming.rs stdout/stderr seq# isolation needs verification
description:
site: crates/m80-guestd/src/connection/streaming.rs:286-299
finder: trim-the-fat r5

Problem: Two capture threads (stdout + stderr) increment per-stream `seq` counters. Likely safe (each thread writes to its own stream-typed frame; counters are per-stream), but worth a quick verification + test that confirms the invariant: stdout_seq and stderr_seq must increment monotonically within their own stream and are independent across streams.

Fix: read the code path carefully. If counters are shared (same Atomic), it's a race. If each thread has its own, document the invariant and add a regression test that runs concurrent stdout+stderr writes and asserts per-stream monotonicity.
notes: root=implementation already used independent per-stream seq counters, but test coverage only proved simple ordering. fix=multi-chunk stdout+stderr regression asserts stdout and stderr each start at seq 0 and advance monotonically independently. test=crates/m80-guestd/tests/streaming_exec.rs::streaming_stdout_and_stderr_sequences_are_independent. verification=cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings; cargo test --workspace; git diff --check

title: M80_DEBUG_WIRE env: dump vsock + firecracker REST traffic at framing layer (dev-only)
description:
Wire-level visibility, on demand, without a rebuild. Today protocol bugs require code edits to add eprintlns at the framing layer. A gated env-var dump would save hours per incident.

## Reference

CLAUDE.md "diagnostics before hypotheses" applies inside the workspace too. Most recent vsock-muxer / readiness investigations would have been minutes shorter with raw frame dumps available on demand.

## Scope

- M80_DEBUG_WIRE=vsock|fcrest|all env var.
- m80-vsock: when vsock set, log every framed message in/out at TRACE level with hex+ascii preview (cap message size).
- m80-firecracker-client: when fcrest set, log every REST request method+path+body+response status+body.
- Always gated; never on in release default; documented as "dev/debug only, do not enable in production".
- Output goes to tracing (RUST_LOG=trace picks it up).

## Out of scope

- Persistent capture/replay (use existing logs).
- Filtering by request_id at this layer (request_id end-to-end bead handles it elsewhere).

## Acceptance

- M80_DEBUG_WIRE=all RUST_LOG=trace m80 launch produces visible frame-level lines.
- Default invocation produces zero such lines.
- README of m80-vsock and m80-firecracker-client document the flag.
notes: Implemented 2026-05-05. Two debug_wire modules (vsock + fcrest), OnceLock-cached env parse, format_wire_preview helper at 1024-byte cap, tracing::trace! emission. 18 unit tests added. README sections in both crates document the env var. Channel::recv path forks under the gate to capture raw NDJSON line — documented inline.

title: Generic Guest Exec Service
description: Purpose: generic in-VM daemon listening on vsock that runs argv with optional cwd/env/stdin and returns stdout/stderr/exit/timing, with optional streaming and PTY modes. Contract: image installs guestd; startup binds exec vsock and signals inverted readiness; one connection/request at a time; envelope read -> exec/pty/shutdown dispatch -> response frames -> fs sync -> close; timeouts and cancellation terminate process groups. title: Performance + benchmark coverage push (latency, throughput, density, distribution)
description:
Super-epic for the 2026-05-08 perf-coverage push. 11 sub-epics, each addressing a class of **performance characterization** that's currently unmeasured at the user-visible bench level. Pattern parallels m80-g0v8 (the e2e correctness push) but for perf: the bench harness produces P50/P95 cold-launch numbers and per-phase wallclocks, but throughput, multi-tenant scaling curves, memory cost per VM, P99/P99.9 distribution shape, comparative numbers vs other VMMs, and most subsystem-specific perf are unwitnessed.

## The pattern (and why it surfaces)

m80 has competitive headline numbers (1117 ms cold launch P50, 274 ms snapshot restore P50, 21 ms warm-pool allocate P50). What we don't have: **how those numbers degrade under load**, **what they cost in RAM and disk**, **where the long tail lives**, **what throughput m80 sustains**, and **how m80 compares to its alternatives**. Real production SLOs are bounded by P99, not P50; capacity planning is bounded by RAM and disk per VM, not just launch latency.

The fix is uniform: **for each class of perf promise, add a benchmark that observes the user-visible value across the relevant dimension** (load, scale, distribution, time, alternative).

## Children

| Child | Class | Items |
|---|---|---|
| **B0** Bench harness improvements | Foundation | 10 |
| **B1** Kernel-boot microsecond decomposition | Latency | 10 |
| **B2** Throughput + saturation | Throughput | 10 |
| **B3** Multi-tenant scaling curves | Density | 10 |
| **B4** Memory benchmarks | RAM cost | 10 |
| **B5** Storage primitives benchmarks | Disk perf | 10 |
| **B6** Snapshot/restore profiling deeper | Restore latency | 10 |
| **B7** Network benchmarks | Network perf | 10 |
| **B8** Cancellation + teardown latency | Cleanup latency | 10 |
| **B9** Comparative benchmarks vs other VMMs | Positioning | 10 |
| **B10** Long-tail / jitter / distribution | Distribution shape | 10 |

Total: 11 sub-epics + ~108 child measurements.

## Dependencies

**B0 (harness improvements) is prerequisite for B3, B6, B10.** Those three need N=1000+, percentile histograms, sweep modes, and stale-state isolation — all gaps in the current `bench-cold-launch.sh`. Marked via `blocks` deps; claimers should land B0 first.

**B1 cross-links m80-av33** (open kernel-boot 785 ms epic). m80-av33 names 4 investigation lanes; B1 is the finer-grained measurement targets those lanes will actually probe (KVM memslots, IRQ chip, devtmpfs, virtio-blk per-device, etc.). They complement; don't duplicate.

**B9 (comparative)** has real setup cost (kata + libkrun runnable). Lowest priority unless positioning numbers are actively wanted.

## Acceptance for super-epic

- All 11 child sub-epics closed.
- Each closes with documented numbers, methodology, and (where applicable) a regression baseline pinned in the repo.
- After close: every user-visible perf claim m80 makes has a benchmark observing it; every regression risk has a tracking metric.

## Out of scope

- Performance optimization itself. This push is *measurement* — optimization comes after we know where the cost actually lives.
- Perf SLOs as binding contracts (we set baselines but don't promise stability of specific numbers).
- Internal-only metrics (those stay in unit tests / dev-time tooling).

## Sources

title: B0: Bench harness improvements (foundation; unblocks B3/B6/B10)
description:
Foundational sub-epic. The current bench harness (scripts/bench-cold-launch.sh + bench-summary.py) produces P50/P95 cold-launch numbers at N=30, but lacks the infrastructure to characterize tail latency (P99/P99.9), perform variable sweeps, isolate against host noise, store baselines for regression detection, or observe concurrent behavior. **Several other sub-epics in this push (B3, B6, B10) cannot be done without B0 landing first.**

## Items (10)

1. N=1000+ mode with histogram output (HdrHistogram or CSV bucket): unlocks P99, P99.9 measurement.
2. Per-phase JSON event stream (timestamp + phase + event=start|end + elapsed_us + attempt): enables flame-graph timeline overlay + per-phase SLO tracking.
3. CPU/NUMA/freq isolation knobs: optional `taskset -c <cores>` + `cpupower frequency-set -g performance` wrapper. Documents "best-effort isolation; expected variance baseline."
4. Sweep table mode: `SWEEP=<var>` to sweep one of {vcpu_count, mem_mib, kernel_kind, image_kind} across cells, emit `sweep-<var>.csv`.
5. Concurrent launch probe: `CONCURRENT=N` mode spawns N parallel admissions, measures wall-time-to-all-ready, emits per-VM tail latencies.
6. Stale-state isolation per-run cache drop: `--cold-isolation` flag drops page caches between runs (`echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches`) for true cold-cold.
7. Confidence intervals + outlier flagging: bootstrap-95% CI on each percentile; flag attempts >2σ from mean; t-test gating for regression.
8. Baseline storage in repo: check in `crates/m80-firecracker/benches/baseline.json`; `bench-summary.py diff` auto-compares; CI gate via `--fail-on-regress 10`.
9. Per-run snapshot to artifact storage: archival of CSVs + phase JSON for historical trend tracking.
10. Warmup parameterization + documentation: expose `WARMUP=N`; document why first 2-3 runs are colder (page cache, TLB, scheduler state).

## Acceptance

- bench-cold-launch.sh accepts new env vars (N, WARMUP, SWEEP, CONCURRENT, --cold-isolation).
- bench-summary.py emits histograms + percentiles {P50, P75, P90, P95, P99, P99.9, max} per phase per cell.
- baseline.json checked in; CI workflow gates merges via configurable threshold.
- Documented in docs/perf/bench-harness.md (or extend cold-launch.md).

## Why this blocks others

- **B3** (multi-tenant scaling): needs CONCURRENT=N + sweep table.
- **B6** (snapshot deeper): needs stale-state isolation + N=1000.
- **B10** (long-tail): needs N=1000 + histograms.
- **B2/B7/B8** benefit from sweep + per-phase JSON for parameter exploration.

## Sources

- 2026-05-08 bench survey, Lens 11.
- scripts/bench-cold-launch.sh + scripts/bench-summary.py (existing harness; gaps identified by survey).

title: B9: Comparative benchmarks vs other VMMs (lower priority — kata + libkrun setup cost)
description:
**Lower-priority sub-epic**: requires running kata-fc + smolvm/libkrun + raw FC alongside m80. Real setup cost (~1-2 days just to get the comparators runnable). Worth doing for positioning numbers but only when actively wanted.

## Standardized workload battery

1. echo hello (minimum exec latency)
2. cat /etc/passwd (file-read latency)
3. python -c 'print(1+1)' (Python startup cost)
4. /bin/true × 1000 (rapid exec rate, throughput)
5. curl https://example.com (network reachability + latency)
6. sha256sum /workspace/large.bin (workspace I/O)
7. cargo build of a known-tiny crate (mixed CPU + I/O + net)

## Comparison axes (per workload, for each VMM)

8. Cold-start latency P50/P95/P99
9. Warm-restore latency where applicable (m80 snapshot, kata template, libkrun has none)
10. Idle RSS + workload RSS + density (concurrent VMs on identical hardware)

## Acceptance

- Comparative table in docs/perf/comparative.md.
- Each cell shows m80 vs raw-FC vs kata-fc vs smolvm-libkrun.
- Identifies where m80's overhead lives (jailer cost, host-side wrapper) and where m80 is intentionally slower (multi-tenant safety) vs fixable.

## Out of scope

- Choosing a VMM based on results. m80 is committed to FC; this is positioning data, not a swap decision.
- Apples-to-oranges comparisons (e.g., libkrun's TSI rootless networking against m80's NAT model — different threat models).

## Sources

- 2026-05-08 bench survey, Lens 9.
- /tank/projects/firecracker/, /tank/projects/kata-containers/, /tank/projects/smolvm/.

title: B1: Kernel-boot microsecond decomposition (extends m80-av33)
description:
**Cross-links m80-av33** (open: 'Attack the 785ms phase_12b_ready_accept'). m80-av33 names 4 investigation lanes (cpu_template, RAM reduction, deeper kernel stripping, KVM-setup measurement); B1 is the finer-grained measurement targets those lanes will probe. Together they decompose the 785 ms ready_accept that dominates cold launch.

## Items (10)

1. KVM memslot establishment cost — Firecracker REST `/vm/memory/mmap` + page-table setup. Measure via `ftrace:kvm_mmio_emulation` + strace on FC. Expected 5-15 ms.
2. IRQ chip + LAPIC initialization — `CreateIrqChip` ioctl + guest `setup_IO_APIC()`. Expected 10-30 ms.
3. CPUID feature advertisement + MSR negotiation — KVM VMX/SVM feature traps + guest probes. Expected 5-20 ms cumulative.
4. devtmpfs mount + device node population — currently bundled into `pseudo_fs_mounted` 5.7 ms delta. Isolate the actual subcost.
5. Virtio-blk discovery and negotiation per device — vda/vdb/vdc each. Expected 2-5 ms per device. Reveals if device init has implicit serialization.
6. Serial console (8250) init cost — `serial8250_isa_init_ports` + baud rate negotiation. Expected 3-10 ms.
7. Kernel cmdline parsing + initcall ordering — simulate with `initcall_debug=1`, parse `dmesg | grep "calling | initcall_"`. Expected 50-150 ms total.
8. TSC calibration + clock source establishment — `calibrate_tsc()` + `clocksource_done_booting()`. Expected 5-25 ms. Check kvmclock vs HPET fallback.
9. ACPI vs MMIO probe time delta — stripped kernel disables ACPI; measure savings. Expected 20-50 ms.
10. Overlayfs mount decomposition — current 2.8 ms delta in pivot_rootfs. Decompose mount syscall + inode cache + lower/upper binding.

## Acceptance

- Each sub-stage is measured via `trace_printk()` / `M80_GUEST_BOOT` milestone / `ftrace` / `strace` as appropriate.
- Results land in docs/perf/cold-launch.md as a "kernel boot decomposition" section.
- Cumulative cost of identified stages accounts for >80% of the 785 ms ready_accept delta.
- Optimization candidates surface (which stages are deferrable, parallelizable, removable).

title: B2: Throughput + saturation benchmarks
description:
m80 has zero published throughput numbers. Latency benchmarks dominate. **Throughput bounds multi-tenant capacity, request-rate ceilings, and bandwidth claims** — none of which are quantified.

## Items (10)

1. file_read MB/s for 100 MB file via chunked transport. Baseline: host pipe to tmpfs.
2. file_write MB/s same payload. Baseline: dd to tmpfs.
3. ExecStdout streaming: bytes/sec from a sustained-output workload (`yes | head -c 500M`). Baseline: host pipe.
4. Concurrent exec capacity per VM: how many concurrent execs can a single VM sustain (vsock multiplexing limits)? P50 latency per turn at N=1, 8, 32.
5. Concurrent-VM saturation: cold launch P50 degradation at N=1 → 8 → 16 → 32 → max. Where does the host saturate first (admission lock / cgroup VFS / mount table)?
6. Pool refill bandwidth: snapshots/sec the warm-pool can sustain under continuous drain.
7. Image-build artifacts/hour: minimal vs ubuntu vs stripped at varied rootfs sizes. Builder throughput governs pool feasibility.
8. Workspace change-extraction MB/s: scratch loop-mount + file-walk + write to host. Bounds writeback throughput.
9. Vsock connection establishment rate: connections/sec until accept loop saturates.
10. Ready-probe stability under sustained admission: P95 of `phase_12b_ready_accept` under launch rate of 1/2/5/10 per second.

## Acceptance

- Each measurement has an explicit baseline (host equivalent or theoretical bound).
- Saturation point and bottleneck identified for each.
- Results in docs/perf/throughput.md (new doc).

## Sources

- 2026-05-08 bench survey, Lens 2.

title: B3: Multi-tenant scaling curves (HIGH LEVERAGE — gates conveyor-belt density claims)
description:
Conveyor-belt strategy targets pools of N=20+ concurrent VMs. **The headline numbers were measured at N=1; how they degrade across N=5/10/25/50/100 is unknown.** This is the most user-impactful gap on the perf coverage list.

**Depends on B0** (harness improvements; needs CONCURRENT=N + sweep modes + N=1000 percentiles).

## Items (10)

1. Cold launch P50/P95/P99 at N={1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100} concurrent VMs. Sweep table.
2. Warm-pool allocate latency at sustained lease rate {1, 5, 10, 25} req/sec.
3. Pool refill backlog: admit 50 VMs, lease all, destroy all concurrently; time to all-ready.
4. Snapshot capture under concurrent VM exec activity. Capture latency vs idle.
5. Cgroup-creation contention at N={5, 25, 100} concurrent admissions. `phase_5b` per-VM degradation.
6. VFS / mount-table lock contention: sustained `mount()` rate; tail latency of mount syscall at N=1/10/50/100 per second.
7. Run-dir creation rate: `phase_1` latency under sustained launch rate.
8. Bridge / TAP creation contention at N=5/25 concurrent network setups.
9. Iptables rule churn: launch P50 with 0 / 100 / 1000 / 10000 existing rules. Does packet processing degrade?
10. Memory accounting accuracy at N=50 concurrent VMs: per-VM cgroup `memory.current` vs `/proc/meminfo` RSS sum delta.

## Acceptance

- Each curve has a knee-point identified (where degradation goes super-linear).
- Bottleneck named for each (resource limit, lock contention locus, pool-sizing rule).
- Results inform conveyor-belt pool sizing recommendations + the m80-c78m saturation bug context.
- Land in docs/perf/scaling.md (new doc).

## Cross-references

- m80-c78m (stress-ng saturation 0% pass) is the open bug surfacing the worst case of this gap.
- Gates the m80-iswt request-path-latency claim (45 ms allocation under load is a B3 measurement).

title: B4: Memory benchmarks (HIGH LEVERAGE — gates 200 tenants × 256 MiB capacity claim)
description:
The conveyor-belt strategy claims 'RAM scales with concurrency, not tenant count' — 10 concurrent × 256 MiB = ~2.5 GiB. **That claim is unmeasured.** Per-VM RSS, lazy-fault percentages, and overhead at scale are blank spots in the capacity model.

## Items (10)

1. Idle baseline RSS: configured 128 MiB VM at rest, post-boot, no workload. FC process VmRSS + guest kernel + m80-guestd.
2. Lazy-fault percentage: how much of memory_mib is actually backed by physical pages after boot? Pre-faulted vs touch-on-access.
3. Workload-driven RSS growth (cargo build of small crate): trajectory over time. Stabilizes? Hits cgroup limit?
4. Per-workload RSS for common cases: echo hello, python -c, curl, sha256sum.
5. Host-side process cost per N VMs: m80-firecracker library, m80-cli RSS scaling.
6. mem.snap disk size vs restored RSS: 256 MiB VM captured = 256 MiB on disk; restored VM RSS — lazy or eager?
7. Conveyor-belt pool RSS sum: N=20 idle generic 128 MiB pool VMs. Theoretical 2.56 GiB; measured?
8. OOM kill latency: when memory.max exceeded, how long until SIGKILL? memory.max_events to process death.
9. Memory pressure under high concurrency: 50 VMs × 256 MiB on 32 GiB host. Swap kicks in? Per-VM degradation observable?
10. Image-build memory peak: m80-image-build host-side RSS for various rootfs sizes.

## Acceptance

- Each measurement has methodology (smaps/RSS/PSS) + expected range.
- Capacity-planning numbers documented: memory cost per VM at common configurations.
- Results in docs/perf/memory.md (new doc).

title: B6: Snapshot/restore profiling deeper (gates warm-pool refill story)
description:
P50 snapshot restore = 274 ms (single number). The breakdown is unmeasured. **Depends on B0** (needs N=1000 + cache-isolation between runs for cold/warm separation).

## Items (10)

1. mem.snap read path: mmap vs pread; lazy-fault vs pre-fault. Which dominates the 274 ms?
2. Capture phase breakdown: pause duration (PATCH Paused) + vm.snap write + mem.snap write + resume. Pause cost specifically — gates live-capture use cases.
3. Scaling vs VM size: 128 / 256 / 512 / 1024 MiB. Bytes/sec read rate. Memory-bound or I/O-bound?
4. File-cache temperature effects: cold (caches flushed) vs warm (mem.snap in page cache) vs partial. Restore latency delta.
5. Concurrent restore from same mem.snap: 5-10 simultaneous, read-only mmap-shared. Latency degradation? Page-fault rate?
6. Vsock probe retry loop breakdown: TRANSPORT_RESET settle time, attempt count, per-attempt open latency. Currently 50 ms sleep / 5 s cap.
7. Snapshot-of-snapshot cost: capture from a restored VM. Differs from first-capture?
8. Capture sustainable rate: snapshots/sec on a single host. Bottleneck: REST serialization, disk write concurrency, kernel mem snapshot logic?
9. Lazy-fault vs pre-fault for mem.snap: posix_madvise(WILLNEED) vs implicit on Resume. Trade-off restore latency vs first-exec latency.
10. Snapshot disk usage + compression trade-offs: 256 MiB VM mem.snap exact size; zstd/gzip ratio + decompress-on-load latency.

## Acceptance

- Concurrent-restore curve published.
- Documented in docs/perf/snapshot.md (extending the existing design doc).

title: B7: Network benchmarks
description:
m80-net-outbound (~3500 LOC, the largest single risk surface) and the new JoinNetns mode have zero throughput / latency benchmarks. NoEgress baseline cost is unmeasured.

## Items (10)

1. AllowOutbound TCP/UDP throughput via iperf3: guest → external. 64B–16MB packet sizes; idle vs loaded host.
2. Round-trip latency (ping): guest → gateway, guest → external. P50/P95/max microseconds.
3. DNS query latency overhead: with vs without m80 DNS allowlist proxy. Cold (first) vs warm (cached) per-query.
4. Iptables rule count scaling: launch P50 with 0 / 100 / 1000 / 10000 existing rules. Packet processing degradation?
5. Concurrent guest bandwidth fairness: N VMs all curl-ing simultaneously. Per-VM mean / P95, Jain index, total.
6. NoEgress packet-drop CPU cost: idle guest, host CPU consumed by netfilter dropping outbound. Cycles per dropped packet.
7. nf_conntrack table fill rate: long-running workload connecting to N hosts. Time to fill default hashsize. Per-VM sustained connection rate.
8. DNS allowlist policy refresh cost: full rule rewrite time + in-flight query disruption.
9. Bridge / TAP setup phase isolation: realize_bridge_and_tap + apply_outbound_nat_policy timing. Currently bundled in `phase_6_network_realize`.
10. AllowOutbound vs JoinNetns parity: same workload (10× curl) on both modes. Per-request latency, throughput, CPU.

## Acceptance

- Each benchmark has tool (iperf3, ping, dnsperf, qperf) + expected range + saturation point.
- Documented in docs/perf/network.md (new doc).

title: B8: Cancellation + teardown latency
description:
Cancellation (m80-lt15.22 closed) and teardown (BoundedStop → ResidueCleanup → Release) have unit tests for correctness but no published latency data.

## Items (10)

1. Cancel-to-exit latency: P50/P95 from CancelRequest to ExecExit for (a) sleep workload, (b) CPU-bound, (c) I/O-bound.
2. Process-group kill efficacy: spawn 5 children via bash; cancel kills all. Time-to-last-child-dead.
3. TERM-then-KILL grace validation: PROCESS_GROUP_TERM_GRACE = 100 ms; verify P99 ≤ 105 ms for cooperative workloads.
4. Streaming exec cancel mid-flight: time from CancelRequest to last-chunk-flushed.
5. BoundedStop RPC timeout (5 s) validation: unresponsive guestd → SIGKILL fires at ~5 s, not before.
6. Run-dir rmdir cost at varied residue: empty / 1 GB overlay / overlay + snapshot binds.
7. End-to-end stop wallclock: BoundedStop / OptionalChangeExtract / ResidueCleanup / Release per-phase decomposition.
8. Force-kill latency (no RPC path): force_kill() to firecracker_pid + jailer_pid both gone.
9. Snapshot capture cancellation: capture mid-flight; cancel; verify atomic or fully reversible.
10. Concurrent stop safety: 10 simultaneous stops; no deadlock, no permit leak.

## Acceptance

- Each path has named P50/P95 number.
- Stop-budget SLO documented (e.g., 'P99 stop in <2 s for cooperative workloads, <6 s including force-kill').
- Land in docs/perf/cleanup.md.

## Sources

- 2026-05-08 bench survey, Lens 8.

title: Hostname egress allowlist for OutboundNat
description:
Add a hostname-based egress allowlist lane to OutboundNat so the user-facing process wrapper can express "this process may reach api.example.com but not the whole internet" without forcing callers to precompute CDN IP ranges.

Reference:
- smolvm-exploration/04-networking-architecture.md: smolvm's allow-host path uses an in-guest DNS proxy over vsock and exact-or-suffix hostname matching. The mechanism is VMM-independent even though smolvm's TSI backend is not.

Scope:
- Design the m80 shape for hostname allowlists alongside existing CIDR policy. Candidate CLI/config vocabulary: `--allow-host <domain>`, `--allow-cidr <cidr>`, and config equivalents under the selected egress profile.
- Guest path: resolv.conf points at a small guest DNS proxy or guestd-owned DNS listener when hostname allowlists are active.
- Host path: DNS queries cross vsock to a host-side filter that exact/suffix matches allowed names, forwards allowed queries to admitted upstream resolvers, and returns NXDOMAIN or another explicit denial for blocked names.
- OutboundNat iptables remains default-deny except admitted DNS and resolved allowed destinations. Unsupported combinations fail closed; no fallback from allow-host to unrestricted outbound.
- Keep this generic network policy. No agent provider presets, no tool-level effect classes, no idempotency semantics.

Acceptance:
- docs/behaviors/network-outbound-nat/hostname-allowlist.md records the DNS flow, match rules, denial behavior, and limitations.
- Unit tests cover exact match, suffix match, near-miss rejection (evilapi.example.com vs api.example.com), malformed DNS, and denied-domain response.
- KVM or fixture test proves `m80 run --egress outbound --allow-host example.com` reaches the allowed host and blocks a non-allowed host, without requiring public internet in default CI.
- Cleanup tests prove DNS proxy state and any iptables additions are removed with the VM.

title: rtnetlink link ops plus no-ip TAP creation in m80-net-outbound
description: Replace planned Command::new(ip) shellouts in m80-net-outbound. Reference: kata-exploration/04-networking-architecture.md shows direct netlink APIs for host link work; Linux tun.c is also part of the contract because current TUN/TAP rtnetlink support permits deletion/introspection but rejects creation. Scope: add rtnetlink workspace dependency; use rtnetlink for bridge add/delete, link get, link MAC set, link up/down, bridge attach, and address assignment; create TAP devices without /sbin/ip by using a safe wrapper over the Linux TUN/TAP driver; keep iptables/sysctl policy work out of this bead; update m80-net-outbound README to document CAP_NET_ADMIN plus the rtnetlink/TUN split. Out of scope: replacing iptables with nftables or a netlink firewall API; ifb/tc-filter work; full bridge ownership/idempotency realization, which remains under m80-exy.3 and children.
acceptance_criteria: m80-net-outbound has a no-ip link-ops path: rtnetlink for bridge/address/link mutation/deletion, TUN/TAP driver for TAP creation. Regression coverage pins tap/bridge lifecycle ordering and asserts the link-ops source contains no /sbin/ip or ip tuntap shellout. An ignored CAP_NET_ADMIN probe exercises real TAP create/delete through the no-/sbin/ip path. README documents the dependency and the kernel reason TAP creation is not rtnetlink.

title: DNS-name allowlist for outbound egress policy
description:
Add a DNS-name egress allowlist lane to OutboundNat so users can constrain world visibility by hostname, not only by precomputed CIDR. CIDR-only policy makes callers chase rotating CDN/IP ranges and weakens the process-wrapper mental model.

Reference: smolvm-exploration/04-networking-architecture.md describes a small guest DNS proxy plus host allowlist filter. m80 keeps Firecracker bridge/tap/NAT, but the DNS-name policy shape is VMM-independent.

Scope:
- Design `--allow-host <name>` / config/API vocabulary and exact-or-suffix matching rules.
- Guest-side DNS proxy on loopback rewrites resolv.conf only when hostname policy is enabled.
- Host-side allowlist service receives DNS queries over vsock, returns upstream answers or NXDOMAIN/refused, and keeps default-deny iptables behavior intact.
- Define interaction with admitted DNS resolvers, raw IP connects, cached DNS, and `--egress none`.
- No HTTP proxy, no TLS MITM, no agent-level tool policy.

Acceptance:
- docs/behaviors/network-outbound-nat/dns-name-allowlist.md documents mechanism, policy, failure modes, and non-goals.
- m80-net-outbound and m80-guestd tests cover allow, suffix allow, deny, malformed query, and cleanup.
- CLI docs/help expose hostname policy as world visibility, not VM network plumbing.
- KVM e2e proves an allowed hostname resolves/connects while a denied hostname fails without weakening `NoEgress`.

title: Storage pivot: shared RO base + per-VM overlay rootfs
description:
Replace the per-VM full file-copy of the base ext4 (Rootfs::clone, ~727 ms on 256 MiB image) with a shared read-only host-side base file plus a per-VM sparse ext4 overlay assembled in-guest as overlayfs. The host file is presented to every VM as drive 1 with is_read_only: true; the per-VM sparse ext4 is drive 2; an optional workspace ext4 becomes drive 3. m80-guestd, running as PID 1 on the minimal-init image, mounts /dev/vda read-only as the lowerdir, /dev/vdb rw as the upperdir/workdir host, assembles overlayfs at a staging mount, then pivot_roots into it before mounting the workspace at /workspace.

WHY: ~700 ms cold-launch saved; per-VM disk drops from O(base size) to O(actual writes). Firecracker docs explicitly bless this pattern (docs/snapshotting/snapshot-support.md:77). m80-urc.1 (per-VM cloning) closed premise-refuted.

PRIORITY NOTE (2026-05-04): P2 after agent-use-case re-rank — snapshot/restore (m80-rrp.3) is the headline cold-launch unlock; this is complementary architectural cleanup + ~700 ms incremental win, queued behind P1.

PLAN: docs/planning/storage-pivot-bead-plan.md (full leaf descriptions). Exploration: docs/exploration/{kata-containers,firecracker-shared-rootfs,overlayfs-kernel-semantics,runc-crun-overlayfs-init,firecracker-containerd}.md.

NON-GOALS: Multi-layer EROFS stacking. Host-side device-mapper thin pools. tmpfs upper layer. Snapshot-resume integration (complementary, m80-rrp.3). Live writeback. Removing ubuntu/systemd image.

title: DESIGN: lock storage API, drive layout, in-guest mount sequence
description:
Produce a written design that pins, in one place, the contract every other leaf in this epic consumes:

1. m80-storage public surface (final form): Rootfs::prepare(base, overlay_dest, overlay_size_bytes), Rootfs::new_at, Rootfs::base_path, Rootfs::overlay_path. Rootfs::clone and Rootfs::path deleted. Caller verifies base sha256; prepare allocates sparse + mkfs.ext4 -F.

2. Drive layout, PUT order: vda=base RO, vdb=overlay RW, vdc=workspace RW (when present). PUT order matches; is_read_only:true on vda; root is vda; ACPI DSDT order is the documented contract (firecracker-shared-rootfs.md §2).

3. In-guest sequence (PID 1): the 11-step mount/pivot pseudocode from overlayfs-kernel-semantics.md is normative — MS_REC|MS_PRIVATE on /, mount vda RO at /lower, vdb at /upper, mkdir /upper/root and /upper/.work, mount overlay at /merged, mount /proc /sys /dev INTO /merged, MS_SLAVE|MS_REC on /, bind /merged onto itself, pivot_root('.','.') per kata, MNT_DETACH old root, then mount /dev/vdc at /workspace inside the new root.

4. Failure policy: overlay mount or pivot failure as PID 1 panics (no kernel panic recovery; run-dir preserved). No retry.

5. Sparse overlay sizing: default 512 MiB sparse; configurable via SandboxConfig::overlay_size_bytes.

ACCEPTANCE: doc landed at docs/design/storage-overlay.md with API signatures, drive table, pseudocode in code blocks. Cross-references to four exploration docs. Both crates/m80-storage/README.md and crates/m80-firecracker/README.md (already drafted) reconciled. No code in this leaf — contract leaf.

EFFORT: S (3-4 hours). Captures decisions made in exploration docs.
notes: doc=docs/design/storage-overlay.md

title: PERF: overlay ext4 template and reflink/copy fallback
description:
Remove the residual per-VM mkfs.ext4 cost from storage prep by cloning a preformatted empty overlay image instead of formatting a fresh sparse ext4 on every launch. This is the follow-up triggered by the measured post-pivot storage_prep cost.

## Current evidence

- Storage pivot removed the full base-rootfs copy, but sparse overlay creation plus mkfs.ext4 still costs about 216 ms P50 for the minimal image.
- docs/design/storage-overlay.md R5 says >100 ms should trigger a cp --reflink=auto template follow-up. That threshold is now hit.

## Scope

- Add an m80-storage path that prepares an empty ext4 overlay template once, then creates per-VM overlay images from it with cp --reflink=auto where supported and plain copy fallback otherwise.
- Preserve the existing hard invariants: the base rootfs is read-only, the per-VM overlay is private, and overlayfs workdir starts empty.
- Template identity must include size and filesystem assumptions so a stale/wrong-size template is a hard error, not silently reused.
- Keep the behavior inside m80-storage/m80-firecracker VM mechanics; no adapter workspace semantics.
- Update preflight if new host assumptions are introduced.

## Non-goals

- Device-mapper thin pools, qcow2, host-side overlayfs, or multi-layer EROFS.
- Optimizing scratch-workspace hydration; this bead is rootfs overlay image creation only.

## Acceptance

- Unit tests cover template creation, reflink success path where available or injectable, plain-copy fallback, size mismatch hard failure, and empty-workdir invariant.
- A focused benchmark shows phase_3_storage_prep before/after and records P50/P95.
- docs/design/storage-overlay.md and crates/m80-storage/README.md document the template contract and failure modes.
- The implementation does not silently create parent directories or tolerate malformed template metadata.

title: PERF: move boot artifact sha verification out of per-launch storage prep
description:
Current evidence after m80-f2zc.10:

- Overlay-template cloning makes `phase_3b_rootfs_prepare` about 13.8 ms P50 on minimal stripped idle.
- Total `phase_3_storage_prep` remains about 180.5 ms P50 because `phase_3a_manifest_verify` is about 166.8 ms P50.
- Loaded phase-bearing attempts show the same shape: manifest verification about 187.9 ms P50 and rootfs prepare about 16.1 ms P50.

Scope:

- Decide and implement a fail-closed placement for full boot artifact sha256 verification that does not rehash every artifact on every launch.
- Preserve the current boot identity invariant: m80 must not boot a kernel/rootfs/guestd artifact that has not been verified against the manifest in this process or admitted trust boundary.
- Make the trust boundary explicit in code and docs: process startup preflight, backend admission, artifact identity cache, or another narrow mechanism.
- Keep hard errors for manifest mismatch, missing artifacts, and stale artifact identity. No silent fallback to unchecked boot.
- Measure before/after with `phase_3a_manifest_verify`, `phase_3_storage_prep`, and total wallclock on minimal stripped idle N>=30; loaded evidence N>=5 or an explicit saturation note is acceptable.

Non-goals:

- Weakening manifest verification semantics to hit a benchmark.
- Adapter-level idempotency or workspace policy.
- Broader overlay artifact pools; `Rootfs::prepare` is already below the 80 ms target.

Acceptance:

- A test fails if a changed/tampered artifact can be launched without a verified identity decision at the selected trust boundary.
- `docs/perf/cold-launch.md` records before/after P50/P95 for `phase_3a_manifest_verify`, `phase_3_storage_prep`, and wallclock.
- The relevant crate README documents the new verification contract.
- No per-launch full rootfs sha256 recompute remains on the normal cold-launch path unless the doc explicitly justifies it as the chosen invariant.

Returns Rootfs { base, overlay }. Add base_path() and overlay_path() accessors. title: IMPL m80-firecracker: three-drive PUT in PUT-order with is_read_only on base
description:
Update boot-phase block-device PUT sequence to:
1. PUT rootfs with is_read_only:true and is_root_device:true, host_path = Rootfs::base_path()
2. PUT rootfs_overlay with is_read_only:false, host_path = Rootfs::overlay_path()
3. PUT workspace with is_read_only:false, host_path = Scratch::path(), only when SandboxConfig::workspace_dir.is_some()

Order is load-bearing: Firecracker assigns vda/vdb/vdc by PUT order (firecracker-shared-rootfs.md §2). Base file is bind-mounted into the jailer chroot exactly as today; nothing changes about the jailer surface beyond an extra bind-mount for the overlay file.

- Integration test (root-required, gated #[ignore]): launch a VM, attach to admin socket, GET drives, assert vda is RO and vdb/vdc are RW.
- README drive-layout table reconciled if needed (already drafted).

title: E2E PTY signal/EOF/resize/raw-mode coverage
description:
m80's PTY mode (-it / --tty -i) has one e2e (interactive_tty_probe_*) that tests ANSI forwarding and exit-code preservation. None of the interactive-UX value-props are pinned:
- SIGINT during read → exit 130 (the standard interactive-cancel path)
- EOF on stdin → workload sees EOF (Ctrl-D pattern)
- SIGWINCH on resize → workload sees new dimensions (vim/htop expect this)
- Raw mode setup (cfmakeraw) — neither smolvm nor m80 does this explicitly per audit; verify behavior

These are user-visible promises of "interactive terminal works." Without e2e, a regression in PTY plumbing surfaces only when a user complains.

## Children
4 child tasks, one per signal/event class.

## Acceptance for the umbrella
- 4 new test functions under crates/m80-firecracker/tests/ (or extend e2e_tty.rs).
- Each verifies the user-visible behavior, not just plumbing existence.

## Sources
- 2026-05-08 conversation.
- crates/m80-firecracker/tests/e2e_tty.rs (existing PTY baseline).
- 20-agent guest-daemon audit Lens S4 (smolvm PTY) for raw-mode reference patterns.
notes: captured PTY signal, Ctrl-D EOF, resize, and host raw-mode e2e coverage. Direct firecracker suite: crates/m80-firecracker/tests/pty_interaction_real_kvm.rs (3 ignored real-KVM tests). CLI suite: crates/m80-cli/tests/e2e_tty.rs (2 ignored real-KVM tests). Fix included guest PID-1 devpts prerequisites: devpts without MS_NODEV and recursive /dev bind through pivot.

title: E2E PTY: raw mode setup verified (cfmakeraw applied)

title: Crate contract cleanup: thin surfaces + exhaustive READMEs
description:
Audit each m80 crate's public surface and clean up the contract so every crate
becomes a black box LLMs (and humans) can reason from the README alone.

Two requirements baked into every leaf:
1. The crate's `README.md` enumerates the FULL public surface — not partial. Every
   `pub` item from `lib.rs` (and CLI/binary contract for binaries) appears with a
   one-line description.
2. The public surface is as thin as possible. Items consumed by 0 or 1 external
   crates that don't have a structural reason to be public become `pub(crate)`.

20 per-crate audits (one sonnet per crate) + 5 cross-crate audits surfaced ~130
specific cleanup actions, each citing file:line and naming files to touch and
acceptance criteria. All audit transcripts are at `/tmp/m80-contracts/`.

Headline numbers from the audit:
- m80-net-outbound: 54 pub items, only ~10 externally consumed (largest thinning target)
- m80-firecracker: ~65 pub items with ~29% README drift; "boot_args_for" doc references a private fn
- m80-firecracker-client: 8 preboot-only structs are single-consumer (m80-firecracker only)
- m80-test-helpers: README absent (P1)
- m80-guestd: README claims "no library API" but a lib target exists with public modules used by 9 integration tests
- m80-net-mode: README has wrong variant name (OutboundNat vs AllowOutbound)
- ConfigError::Other(String) used at 32+ call sites — the most pervasive doctrine violation
- 4 vocabulary inconsistencies (fc_socket vs api_socket, fc_pid vs firecracker_pid, etc.)
- 1 duplicate re-export, 4 cross-crate re-exports that need decisions, 7 raw-literal sites that should use existing constants

Acceptance for the super-epic: after every child closes, every crate's README
exhaustively lists its public surface, every pub item has at least 2 external
consumers OR an explicit comment naming why it stays public, and the workspace
has zero `Other(String)` / `Generic(String)` catch-all error variants.
close_reason: captured: all crate-contract cleanup children closed; README/public-surface cleanup and error doctrine validated; workspace clippy/check/tests and catch-all rg gate passed

title: E2E file-op error path coverage (typed FileError variants)
description:
m80's wire file ops (read_file, write_file, list_dir, stat_file, remove_file, FileMkdir, chunked write) exist *because* they surface typed FileError responses (PermissionDenied, NotFound, IoError, InvalidPath) instead of stderr-text + exit-code from exec. **None of those error variants are e2e-pinned.** A refactor that collapses "file not found" into "io error" would pass current tests because all e2e file-op tests are happy-path-only.

This is exactly the writeback-shape gap: typed errors are the value-prop, but the negative paths aren't behaviorally verified.

## Children
5 child tasks, one per major error variant or pattern. Each is a small real-KVM e2e that triggers the error condition and asserts the typed response.

## Acceptance for the umbrella
- All major FileError variants have at least one e2e that triggers them and asserts the typed surface.
- A regression that maps PermissionDenied → IoError surfaces as a named test failure.

## Sources
- 2026-05-08 conversation; e2e gap survey.
- crates/m80-proto/src/error.rs (FileError variants).
- crates/m80-firecracker/tests/end_to_end_real_kvm.rs:163-282 (existing happy-path file-op tests).

title: End-to-end behavioral verification (proof-of-correctness for user-visible promises)
description:
Super-epic capturing the 2026-05-08 e2e coverage push. Five child epics, each addressing a class of **user-visible promise** that has unit-tested logic but no e2e to pin the observable behavior. Pattern surfaced by the writeback discovery: typed enum / policy / mode → unit test passes the gate → e2e doesn't observe the host-side outcome → a refactor that silently inverts the gate ships green.

## The pattern (and why it keeps appearing)

m80 is built on typed contracts: `WritebackMode`, `EgressMode`, `FileError`, lifecycle modes, identity-verification kill, cgroup limits. Each typed contract has a unit-tested decision function. None of those unit tests **observe the host-side or user-visible result** — the actual file on disk, the actual network reachability, the actual exit code, the actual VM kill, the actual OOM. That observation is exclusively an e2e concern, and the e2e suite has historically grown around the happy path.

The fix is uniform: **for each typed promise, add an e2e that triggers the condition and asserts the user-visible outcome**. Cheap to write per case (~50-100 LOC each); cumulative effect closes a real regression-risk class.

## Child epics

| Child | Class of promise | Children count |
|---|---|---|
| **m80-kd90** | Writeback × exit-code matrix (3 modes × 2 exit codes) | 3 tasks |
| **m80-mx2t** | EgressMode × isolation matrix (3 modes; positive + negative) | 3 tasks |
| **m80-fwy9** | File-op typed error variants (NotFound, PermissionDenied, sequence violations) | 5 tasks |
| **m80-fb2t** | PTY signal/EOF/resize/raw-mode interactive UX | 4 tasks |
| **m80-5vlb** | Closed-epic structural-only coverage cleanup (identity-mismatch kill, cgroup OOM enforcement, snapshot edges, mid-stream cancel, PoolEmpty, idle edges, diagnostic markers) | 7 tasks |

Total: 5 epics + 22 child tasks = **27 beads** in this push.

## Acceptance for the super-epic

- All 5 child epics closed.
- After close: every user-visible promise from a typed-policy / typed-error / lifecycle-mode contract has at least one e2e that **observes the user-visible outcome**, not just the plumbing.
- A regression that inverts a typed-policy gate or collapses a typed-error variant fails a named test.

## Out of scope

- Adding new behavior to m80. This is verifying behavior we already think we have.
- Coverage of internal-only invariants (those stay in unit tests).
- Performance / latency assertions (m80-av33 + bench harness handle that).

## Sources

- 2026-05-08 conversation: writeback sanity check → noticed e2e gap → systematic survey → 5-epic push.
- Each child epic carries its own per-class context, audit references, and acceptance.

title: L1: Lifecycle phase failures + recovery
description:
m80's launch is multi-phase (admission → preflight → manifest → jailer → cgroup → storage → instance-config → drive PUT → boot-args → instance-start → ready) and stop is multi-phase (BoundedStop → OptionalChangeExtract → ResidueCleanup → Release). Each phase can fail; the lifecycle promises typed errors, partial-state cleanup, and permit release. None of the failure-paths are currently triggered at e2e — only the happy path is covered.

## Items

1. GuestdNotReady timeout (phase_12b_ready_accept) — mock stalled guestd; verify FcError::GuestdReadyTimeout, partial state cleaned, permit released.
2. ApiSocketTimeout (phase_10) — delay FC socket past budget; verify FcError::ApiSocketTimeout + cleanup.
3. phase_5b_cgroup_create failure mid-launch — mock subtree creation failure; verify partial state (jail/FC pid) cleaned, permit released.
4. StopDisposition transitions — both NormalStop and ForceKill execute; exit_reason differs in diagnostics.
5. CleanupPhase mid-phase partial failures — BoundedStop fails; ResidueCleanup + Release still execute, permit always released.
6. ForcedKillAmbiguous blocker — kill returns EPERM; CleanupReleaseBlocker::ForcedKillAmbiguous diagnostic; permit NOT released.
7. extract_changes after unclean stop — large streaming exec, cancel mid-stream, stop, extract; ChangeSet coherent or fails cleanly.

## Acceptance for sub-epic
- 7 e2e tests under crates/m80-firecracker/tests/.
- #[ignore = real KVM] or fault-injection where appropriate.
- Regression that inverts cleanup-gating fails a named test.

## Sources
- 2026-05-08 e2e gap survey, Lens 1.
- crates/m80-firecracker/src/{launch.rs,lifecycle.rs,error.rs}.

title: L11: Defense-in-depth security verification (Layer 1 audit + Layer 2 malicious-runner battery)
description:
m80 promises two layers of isolation:

- **Layer 1 (VM isolation)**: the guest workload cannot escape into m80's host process or read host memory/state outside what FC explicitly exposes. This is *inherited* from KVM + Intel/AMD virtualization extensions + FC's VMM design — m80 doesn't implement it, but does control the configuration that activates it.
- **Layer 2 (jailer as defense-in-depth)**: even if Layer 1 is breached and the FC process is fully compromised by an attacker, the jailer constrains what damage they can do on the host. **This is m80-owned and rigorously testable.**

Today neither layer has a deliberately-adversarial test suite. The other test-coverage sub-epics (L1-L10) verify happy-path + typed-error behaviors; this sub-epic verifies the **negative-space** security promises.

## Layer 1 testing strategy

Property "no guest escape" is unenumerable. Instead test:
- **Configuration audit** — FC config exposes the expected isolation properties (cpu_template, MSR allowlist, no IOMMU passthrough, no KVM_CAP_DEBUGREGS for guest, vsock-only-no-other-virtio-pci).
- **Known-CVE smoke battery** — boot a known-curious workload that *tries* publicly-known KVM/virtio escape primitives (open `/dev/mem`, write virtio rings from guest, `rdmsr` host-only MSRs); each must fail with the expected kernel error.
- **CVE version tracking** — FC binary version is at-or-above patches for known CVEs (track via a versioned allowlist).

Failure of any Layer 1 test means the kernel is broken or FC is misconfigured — not that m80 is broken. But m80 is responsible for surfacing the failure before users hit it.

## Layer 2 testing strategy: the malicious-runner pattern

Substitute a deliberately-malicious binary for FC in the jailer's exec slot. Run it through the same jail materialization FC would have used. Each attack attempt asserts the jail held.

This is how kata, Firecracker, and gVisor verify their isolation claims — well-trodden ground.

```rust
// crates/m80-attack-runner/src/main.rs
fn main() {
    let attack = std::env::args().nth(1).unwrap();
    let result = match attack.as_str() {
        "chroot_escape_via_dotdot"  => try_escape_chroot(),
        "read_host_proc_kcore"      => try_read_proc_kcore(),
        "signal_host_pid"           => try_kill_host_pid(),
        // ... ~30 attacks
        _ => panic!("unknown attack"),
    };
    match result {
        Ok(()) => std::process::exit(0),  // BREACHED — test fails
        Err(reason) => { eprintln!("{reason:?}"); std::process::exit(1); }  // jail held — test passes
    }
}
```

Test harness asserts `exit != 0` for each attack. A failing test means a specific named escape vector is no longer blocked.

## Children (11)

- L11.1 — `m80-attack-runner` crate (the malicious binary; ~30 attacks)
- L11.2 — Test harness wiring (jailer materialize + attack-runner exec integration)
- L11.3 — Layer 1: FC configuration audit (cpu_template, MSRs, devices, etc.)
- L11.4 — Layer 1: known-CVE smoke battery (~5-10 published primitives)
- L11.5 — Layer 2: filesystem escape battery (~6 attacks)
- L11.6 — Layer 2: process/PID isolation battery (~5 attacks)
- L11.7 — Layer 2: network isolation battery (~5 attacks)
- L11.8 — Layer 2: privilege escalation battery (~6 attacks)
- L11.9 — Layer 2: resource exhaustion battery (~4 attacks)
- L11.10 — Layer 2: cross-tenant isolation battery (~3 attacks)
- L11.11 — Composition test: assume Layer 1 breach, verify Layer 2 holds standalone

## Acceptance for sub-epic

- `m80-attack-runner` crate exists with ~30 attack primitives.
- Each Layer 2 attack has a named test that asserts the jail blocked it.
- Layer 1 audit tests pin FC config + known-CVE coverage at named version boundaries.
- Composition test verifies that "compromised FC inside m80's jailer" is bounded — no host filesystem reach, no other-tenant access, no privilege escalation, no resource starvation.
- Test failure messages name the specific escape vector that broke (e.g., `jail breached: chroot escape via dotdot succeeded`).

## Out of scope

- Provably-no-escape claim (impossible).
- Hardware-level attestation (TEE/SEV/TDX) — out of m80 scope per CLAUDE.md.
- Fuzz testing of vsock or virtio (separate effort; complementary).

## Sources

- 2026-05-08 conversation: defense-in-depth testing pattern.
- Kata's escape battery: /tank/projects/kata-containers/tests/.
- Firecracker's security tests: /tank/projects/firecracker/tests/.
- gVisor's runsc syscall tests (reference pattern).

title: L11 blocker: define compromised-VMM network namespace policy
description:
The L11 network isolation battery cannot honestly assert all m80-attack-runner network primitives exit non-zero until m80 decides the Layer-2 network boundary for a compromised Firecracker process. Today the official jailer path does not create a private network namespace by default; JoinNetns intentionally places Firecracker in caller-provided network state. Attacks such as listen_all_interfaces or public TCP connect may succeed as ordinary host networking, which would make the planned battery red for a real design reason rather than a test harness issue.

Acceptance:
- Decide and document the Layer-2 network boundary for a compromised Firecracker process in NoEgress/AllowOutbound/JoinNetns modes.
- If the boundary is private-netns-by-default, implement launch/jailer wiring and cleanup.
- If some modes intentionally allow host/caller netns access, rewrite m80-g0v8.11.7 to assert the narrower promised boundary instead of all network primitives.
- Add/adjust ignored defense_in_depth tests only after the policy is explicit.

The L11 resource exhaustion battery needs the attack-runner process to be enrolled in the same cgroup constraints that m80-firecracker applies to Firecracker after jailer launch. description:
Each attack runs inside the jail via m80-attack-runner. Asserts exit != 0.

- chroot_escape_via_dotdot — chdir then ../../../etc; assert no /etc/passwd reachable.

title: Layer 2 battery: privileged network operation isolation
description:
Each attack runs inside the jail via m80-attack-runner and asserts exit != 0 for the current compromised-VMM network boundary. This battery intentionally covers privileged network operations blocked by jailer hardening/capability drop, not ordinary host-namespace TCP/UDP egress.

Attacks:
- open_raw_socket: socket(AF_INET, SOCK_RAW) must fail with EPERM.
- raw_packet_inject: socket(AF_PACKET, SOCK_RAW) must fail with EPERM.
- send_arbitrary_netlink: attempt RTM_NEWLINK/RTM_SETLINK-style mutation must fail with EPERM or equivalent kernel rejection.
- bind_on_host_interface: bind/address a host-only interface name that is not present in the jailed view; assert ENODEV/EADDRNOTAVAIL or equivalent local failure.
- privileged_route_mutation: attempt to add/change a route must fail with EPERM.

Non-assertions under the current policy: listen_all_interfaces and public TCP connect are allowed to succeed for a compromised VMM process in NoEgress/AllowOutbound because those modes are guest networking policies, not private VMM network namespaces. JoinNetns tests assert placement in the caller namespace rather than m80-owned egress semantics.

title: L12: Adversarial guestd harness — real-KVM guest->host wire coverage
description:
L2 (closed) covers wire-protocol negative-space via synthetic-peer mocks and host-side injection of malformed host->guest control data mid-stream. Its close note records the gap: real-KVM end-to-end tests cannot synthesize corrupted **guest->host** response frames without a controlled malicious-guestd. Synthetic peer mocks cover the API-level direction symmetry; only an adversarial guestd binary can produce hostile wire output that traverses the actual vsock + framing + envelope path on a real VM.

This is the parallel pattern to L11 (malicious-runner): substitute a deliberately-adversarial controlled binary for the trusted artifact, then assert the host's typed-error + teardown + diagnostic surface holds. L11 substitutes an attack-runner for the user's program inside the jail; L12 substitutes a malicious-guestd for m80-guestd inside the VM.

## Scope

Real-KVM end-to-end tests where a controlled m80-guestd-malicious binary (cargo feature or separate test-only crate) emits hostile guest->host frames per scenario:

- Framing-level attacks (length-prefix, truncation, alignment)
- Wire-schema attacks (unknown variant tags, mismatched response shapes)
- Semantic attacks (wrong request_id, unsolicited responses, response without preceding request)
- Resource-exhaustion attacks (unsolicited flood, slowloris, no-progress payloads)

Each attack asserts: (a) the host returns a finite typed error variant naming the failure class, (b) the run-dir diagnostic surface records what happened (no silent corruption), (c) the affected channel/sandbox tears down cleanly without resource leaks.

## Why this is not a duplicate of L2

L2 used synthetic peer mocks (m80-vsock test fixtures) and host-side mid-stream injection. Those cover the API-level surface and host->guest direction. The remaining gap is real-KVM guest->host adversarial output: only reachable by running a hostile guestd inside an actual VM. L12 fills that gap and re-runs a subset of L2 scenarios through the real-KVM path with a malicious peer.

## Out of scope

- Attacks at the workload layer (covered by L11 malicious-runner).
- Adding new typed-error variants — L12 verifies the existing surface holds; if a scenario requires a new variant, that is captured as a follow-on bead under m80-2ggw or its own epic.
- Performance/timing assertions — covered by m80-av33 + bench harness.

## Acceptance for sub-epic

- m80-guestd-malicious build artifact exists, attack mode selectable via env var or CLI, feature-gated to keep release builds clean.
- 7+ real-KVM e2e tests under crates/m80-firecracker/tests/ exercising each attack class.
- Each test asserts: typed-error variant + diagnostic marker + clean teardown (verified via run-dir inspection + permit release).
- Coverage map doc records: which adversarial scenarios are covered, which residual gaps remain (e.g., bogus exec exit codes the host has no end-to-end way to verify without a runtime cross-check).

## Sources

- m80-g0v8.2 close note: caveat on m80-g0v8.2.2 explicitly records the malicious guest->host harness gap.
- L11 malicious-runner pattern: same shape applied to a different layer.
- 2026-05-08 e2e gap survey under m80-g0v8.

title: L12.8 — DoS: unsolicited message flood and slowloris
description:
Two adversarial DoS scenarios:
- Flood: malicious guestd sends N unsolicited messages back-to-back (where N is large enough to test rate-limit or backpressure surfaces).
- Slowloris: malicious guestd opens a request slot, writes a few bytes, then stalls indefinitely without completing or closing.

Host must rate-limit, time out, or tear down — depending on documented policy. The test pins the documented policy.

title: L12.9 — Coverage map: real-KVM adversarial guest->host scenarios
description:
Single doc capturing the coverage matrix: which adversarial guest->host scenarios are exercised in real-KVM (via L12), which are exercised only at the synthetic-peer layer (via L2), and which remain residual gaps that no harness can practically reach.

Specifically document residual gaps:
- Bogus exec exit codes / stdout content claims: host has no end-to-end runtime way to verify the workload actually exited as the guest claims, without a runtime cross-check (which we do not currently implement). Document this as a known limitation.
- Wall-clock-coordinated attacks: the malicious peer attempting to exploit timing windows (race against host's reader). Captures whether L12 attempts these or defers them.

title: L2: Wire protocol + transport robustness
description:
Wire protocol (m80-proto + m80-vsock) has unit + round-trip tests but lacks e2e that pins typed-error surface under adversarial conditions: version mismatch, malformed frames, stale request_ids, frame-length boundaries, mid-stream disconnects, cancel races.

## Items

1. Version mismatch — host sends PROTOCOL_VERSION+1; verify typed UnsupportedVersion at the CLI boundary (not silent corruption).
2. Malformed frame mid-stream — mid-streaming-exec, peer sends garbage frame; host gracefully maps to user-visible error.
3. request_id mismatch — peer sends response with wrong request_id; verify typed handling (not silent).
4. Frame-length boundary — payload exactly at MAX_FRAME_BYTES vs +1; round-trip + rejection edges pinned.
5. Forward-compat schema probe — older binary receives future-version envelope; behavior pinned (probably reject).
6. Disconnect mid-streaming-exec — peer drops channel during ExecStdout chunks; typed DisconnectBeforeTerminal with correct context label.
7. Cancel-then-disconnect race — cancel sent, then channel closes before CancelResponse; clean handling.
8. Multi-connection cancel contract — opening a second Channel for cancel (against the documented same-connection contract); behavior pinned.

## Acceptance for sub-epic
- 8 e2e tests under crates/m80-firecracker/tests/ or crates/m80-vsock/tests/ (depending on layer).
- Each negative scenario fails with a named test if the typed-error surface regresses.

## Sources
- 2026-05-08 e2e gap survey, Lens 2.
- crates/m80-proto/src/, crates/m80-vsock/src/, crates/m80-firecracker/src/lifecycle/protocol.rs.

title: L3: m80-jailer materialize + recovery
description:
m80-jailer's plan-as-data + jailer-plan.json + jailer-state.json + recover.rs orphan inspection is a documented advantage over FC's stock jailer. The advantage is not pinned by crash-injection or partial-failure e2e. If these primitives regress silently, the m80-vs-FC narrative breaks.

## Items

1. Partial-failure reversal under Drop — inject failure mid-bind (plan step 4 of N); verify Drop reverses 1-3 + recover.rs sees no residue.
2. State-file atomicity across crashes — SIGKILL during state_json write; recover.rs sees plan + missing-or-partial state, decides correctly.
3. Recovery of mid-launch orphans (firecracker.pid timeout) — mock jailer that never writes pid; verify jail_path residue intact, recover returns NoJail.
4. Device node major/minor verification (m80-16oi closed) — stat /dev/{kvm,net/tun,urandom} inside chroot; major/minor match official values.
5. Mount-NS exit ordering — Drop runs in host mount NS, not jailed; pin by reading /proc/<fc-pid>/ns/mnt before stop, host /proc/self/ns/mnt after stop.
6. Read-only chroot enforcement — inside jailed FC, attempt mount -o remount,rw / and stat /etc/passwd; both must fail.
7. Directory permissions (0o700 + chown) — fork as UID != jailed_uid, attempt to read jail_path; must fail EACCES.
8. Placeholder file cleanup on partial bind failure — inject bind failure on Nth bind; placeholder for prior bind cleaned up; no stray empty files.
9. Inherited hardening applied to FC (m80-jailer-harden) — read /proc/<fc-pid>/status NoNewPrivs/CapAmb/SigBlk/Groups after launch; verify the hardening propagated through to FC, not just the wrapper.
10. Jailer-PID sentinel (0) and daemonized reaping — daemonize=true; jailer-state.json jailer_pid=0; kill(0,SIGKILL) returns ESRCH; recover sees LiveJail with jailer_pid=0.

## Acceptance for sub-epic
- 10 tests under crates/m80-jailer/tests/ or crates/m80-firecracker/tests/.
- Crash-injection / partial-failure tests use deliberate mid-step failure injection.

## Sources
- 2026-05-08 e2e gap survey, Lens 3.
- crates/m80-jailer/src/{plan.rs,materialized.rs,recover.rs}, crates/m80-jailer-harden/src/.

title: L4: Image build + manifest verification
description:
m80-image-build constructs artifacts (kernel + rootfs + guestd) and m80-image-manifest + m80-preflight verify them. Unit tests cover schema and individual build steps; no e2e ties manifest verification to actual launch failure modes when artifacts are tampered, missing, or schema-evolved.

## Items

1. Stripped-kernel determinism — same input → same vmlinux sha; e2e builds twice and compares.
2. Manifest SHA mismatch at preflight — modify rootfs after manifest write; m80 launch fails before guest with FcError::Manifest(Sha256Mismatch{...}).
3. Unknown manifest field rejection — inject "future_field" into manifest; preflight surfaces typed parse error (not silent acceptance).
4. Image-kind dispatch (Minimal vs Ubuntu) — both kinds boot and exec a smoke command; per-kind boot args + systemd-vs-PID-1 differences verified.
5. Schema-version forward-incompatibility — set schema_version=99; preflight typed UnsupportedSchemaVersion(99) (not generic parse error).

title: L5: cgroup limit ENFORCEMENT (not just configured)
description:
**Most concerning sub-epic of the survey.** m80 *configures* cgroup limits (writes to /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.max etc.) and unit tests verify the file-write. **No test verifies any limit is actually enforced by the kernel.** A regression that drops the controller-enable would pass all current tests. Fork-bomb / fd-exhaustion / I/O-throttle are user-visible promises but currently unwitnessed.

m80-5vlb.3 covers memory.max → OOM-kill. This sub-epic covers the rest.

## Items

1. pids.max fork-bomb enforcement — workload runs `:(){ :|:& };:`-style fork bomb; kernel returns EAGAIN at the cap (not runaway tree).
2. io.max / io.weight throttling — io.max wbps=1M; sustained dd write throughput < 1.5M/s; io.stat throttle_ms increments.
3. cpuset.cpus / cpuset.mems pinning — cpuset.cpus=0; /proc/<fc-pid>/status Cpus_allowed_list: 0; affinity held under load.
4. cgroup.subtree_control propagation — read cgroup.subtree_control at every parent; each contains +cpu, +memory, +pids, +io.
5. cgroup cleanup on Drop with live procs — interrupt mid-exec; cgroup.procs non-empty; Drop logs warn + does NOT rmdir; after kill, cleanup succeeds.
6. CLONE_NEWCGROUP namespace isolation — new_cgroup_ns=true; FC sees /proc/self/cgroup with no parent prefix (just "/" at root).

## Acceptance for sub-epic
- 6 tests under crates/m80-cgroup/tests/ or crates/m80-firecracker/tests/.
- Each verifies kernel ENFORCEMENT, not just file-was-written.

## Sources
- 2026-05-08 e2e gap survey, Lens 5.
- crates/m80-cgroup/src/, crates/m80-jailer-harden/src/.

title: L6: m80-storage overlay edge behaviors
description:
m80-storage's overlay+pivot_root model has unit tests for individual primitives (sparseness, mount flags, scratch sizing) but lacks e2e for the actual filesystem-level guarantees: immutability of the lower layer, growth behavior, deferred mkfs, per-image-kind assembly, three-drive PUT order.

m80-kd90 covers the writeback policy. m80-5vlb.3 covers cgroup OOM. This sub-epic is the lower-level storage primitives.

## Items

1. Overlay sparseness — du --apparent-size vs du actual size differ significantly for both template and cloned overlay (verifies fallocate -d worked).
2. Permission preservation through extraction — guest writes file with mode 0700/0644/0400; host stat shows same mode after extract.
3. Overlay immutability: write-to-lower — workload writes to /usr/bin/false (exists in lower); host base unchanged, write landed in upper layer only.
4. Overlay growth under sustained writes — guest writes 10 MiB to /workspace; host overlay file growth matches accumulation (verifies non-pre-allocated semantics).
5. mkfs deferred-until-first-write — workspace device unformatted at boot; first guest write triggers mkfs; verify lazy mkfs vs eager.
6. Overlay assembly per image kind — both minimal and ubuntu boot through 9-step pivot; /lower readable, /upper writable, /merged correct, /workspace mounted post-pivot.
7. Three-drive PUT order — vda RO base + vdb RW overlay + vdc workspace; misordered drives → boot fails or base preserved (no silent corruption).
8. Reflink vs copy fallback — clone on non-reflink-capable FS still succeeds via fallback; both paths produce nlink == 1.
9. Scratch sizing boundary cases — recommended_size honors caps; oversized request bounded; partial mkfs failure cleaned.

## Acceptance for sub-epic
- 9 tests under crates/m80-storage/tests/ + crates/m80-firecracker/tests/.

## Sources
- 2026-05-08 e2e gap survey, Lens 6.
- crates/m80-storage/src/{rootfs.rs,scratch.rs}, crates/m80-guestd/src/pid_one.rs.

title: L7: m80-net-outbound iptables/bridge/DNS lifecycle
description:
m80-net-outbound (~3500 LOC, the largest single risk surface) has unit tests for iptables rule placement, bridge creation, DNS injection. Higher-level mode behavior is m80-mx2t. This sub-epic covers the lower-level invariants: collision detection, drift, idempotent setup, lifecycle of forwarding rules / NAT / TAP / bridge.

## Items

1. Concurrent VM launch IP collision — N=3+ VMs launched concurrently with state-file-based allocation; no racy duplicate-address allocation.
2. Host route collision typing — pre-create route 172.16.0.0/12 on host; m80 launch errors with NetError::HostRouteCollision before any link mutation.
3. Iptables rule drift detection — external process adds rule into m80-owned chain; m80 cleanup detects and surfaces ForeignChainRule (not silent skip or blanket delete).
4. Forwarding entry rules lifecycle — ip_forward sysctl persists across teardown (not reverted; persistent host state).
5. Cleanup-on-failed-launch partial bridge — bridge created, TAP create fails; bridge deleted, no orphan.
6. Orphan TAP detection and recovery — TAP exists, VM state file missing; recover cleans TAP.
7. Idempotent setup — re-run setup on existing bridge handles cleanly; kernel-deleted bridge re-created.
8. NAT masquerade rule lifecycle — created on launch, removed on teardown; foreign nat rules block cleanup with typed error.

## Acceptance for sub-epic
- 8 tests under crates/m80-net-outbound/tests/.
- Concurrent-launch tests use barrier-synchronized threads.
- Foreign-rule tests inject rules via MockPolicyOps or live iptables in CI.

title: L8: m80-preflight capability detection completeness
description:
m80-preflight should fail fast with typed errors before launch when host setup is incomplete. Several capabilities are missing from preflight checks despite being required for launch — failures surface as cryptic launch-time errors instead of clean preflight rejections.

## Items

1. /dev/kvm missing — preflight typed error pointing user at "enable KVM" (not later cryptic open() error).
2. /dev/kvm permission-denied (open(O_RDWR) → EACCES) — typed error vs later fail.
3. KVM CPU flags (vmx/svm) collected but never validated — virtualization unsupported even with /dev/kvm; add typed PreflightError::KvmCpuExtensionMissing.
4. Vsock module missing — env.rs probes vhost_vsock but preflight ignores it; required for guest IPC.
5. TUN module missing — required for AllowOutbound but no preflight check.
6. nf_conntrack module missing — required for NAT but no detection anywhere.
7. Cgroup v2 availability — checked at launch phase 5 (after 4 phases of work), not preflight; surface typed PreflightError::CgroupV2Unavailable at preflight.
8. m80 --json env JSON shape on broken preflight — schema stable on error path (not just happy path); test PreflightDump fields when checks fail.

## Acceptance for sub-epic
- 8 tests under crates/m80-preflight/tests/ + crates/m80-cli/tests/.
- Mock-host-state tests refactor checks into testable fns parameterized by mocked readers.

title: L9: Multi-VM concurrency + race conditions
description:
**Most subtle sub-epic of the survey.** m80 is multi-tenant by design — many VMs may be in flight simultaneously. The behaviors that matter under concurrent load aren't pinned by single-VM e2e. These race conditions are also the cases most likely to bite under real load and not under a unit test.

m80-5vlb.5 covers PoolEmpty single case. This sub-epic covers the harder concurrency questions.

## Items

1. Admission semaphore N+1 concurrent overflow — barrier-synchronized N+1 threads call admit(); exactly N enter, +1 returns AdmissionRefused.
2. Permit return on launch panic mid-flight — panic injection during phase_3/4/11; semaphore restored, second admit succeeds.
3. Concurrent stop + concurrent launch on same run_dir — VM-A stop racing VM-B launch (same vm_id reused); ownership.lock atomicity holds.
4. Recovery loop running mid-launch of fresh VM — background recover.rs while a launch is mid-flight; doesn't kill the fresh VM.
5. Two cancel requests to same exec idempotent + race-safe — both responses arrive; second is AlreadyExited or reflects first cancel.
6. Warm-pool simultaneous lease + refill race — last 2 ready slots leased by 2 threads; refill restarts; both leases succeed.
7. Snapshot + launch concurrency — VM-A captures while VM-B launches from same snapshot parent; no deadlock or partial overwrite.
8. Persistent-VM concurrent exec serialization — Arc<RunningSandbox> with two threads attempting exec — must not compile (Send-bound) or fail safely.

## Acceptance for sub-epic
- 8 tests using barrier-synchronized threading primitives (Arc<Barrier>, parking_lot::Condvar).
- Each captures a specific race window with deterministic synchronization.

## Sources
- 2026-05-08 e2e gap survey, Lens 9.
- crates/m80-firecracker/src/{backend.rs,launch.rs,warm_pool.rs,runroot.rs}.

title: Audit: typed error variants visible at m80-cli + m80-firecracker public surface (no string collapse)
description:
Sweep public error surfaces and ensure typed thiserror variants stay typed at the boundary. Don't collapse to string-wrapped Other / Generic on the way out (kata's mistake at the ttRPC shim boundary).

## Reference

kata-exploration/07-public-api-and-shim.md. Kata's internal errors are typed (ContainerNotFound, ProcessNotFound, AgentConnectionClosed), but at the shim boundary they collapse to ttrpc::Error::Others(string) — losing type information for consumers. m80 should not repeat this.

## Why

CLAUDE.md ("What we don't want") forbids reclassification that hides which call site lost the file; the same principle applies to error type collapse. m80-cli's class-based exit codes (EXIT_PREFLIGHT=2 etc.) only work if the underlying error variants are still discriminable.

## Scope

- Audit m80-firecracker public Error type: are all variants concrete? any "Other(String)" / "Generic"?
- Audit m80-cli error mapping (m80-cli/src/errors.rs): does every internal error variant map cleanly to an exit code, or do some funnel through a string wrapper?
- Where collapse exists, replace with concrete variants.
- Document the policy in CLAUDE.md ("What we don't want") if not already covered.

## Out of scope

- Internal-only error types (those can be richer; the audit is at the public boundary only).
- anyhow at binary edges is fine (that's already the policy).

## Acceptance

- m80-firecracker::Error has no String-wrapping fallback variant (or has one with a written justification).
- m80-cli error → exit-code mapping is exhaustive over the underlying error type (compile-time match coverage).
- One regression test pins at least one specific error → specific exit code.
